Gentry and Chilton argue that "harlot" is the Old Testament's main word for unfaithful Jerusalem (Ezekiel 16; 23) and implies a covenant partner who has broken faith, which a pagan city never was.
The seductive world system of every age that draws people away from God by luxury, power and false religion (Hendriksen).
The apostate church of Rome, unfaithful to Christ her husband (Reformers, Elliott, Barnes).
Walvoord identifies her with a future apostate world religion, which the Antichrist first uses and then destroys.
Who sits on many waters

Jeremiah 51:13 addresses Babylon as the one who dwells by many waters, referring to the Euphrates and its canals. Waters are peoples in Isaiah 8:7 and 17:12-13. Revelation 17:15 explains them as "peoples, multitudes, nations and tongues", the fourfold formula used throughout the book (5:9; 7:9; 13:7).
Rome's empire was built on Mediterranean sea power; the Vespasian coin of Roma on seven hills shows the Tiber at her feet.
The prostitute rules over and depends on the peoples of the world. The image is borrowed from the literal geography of ancient Babylon and given an international meaning.
Gentry answers the objection that Jerusalem did not rule nations: the waters represent Jerusalem's influence over the Jewish diaspora throughout the empire and her political standing with Rome.
The worldwide extent of the end-time religious-political system.
The universal reach of worldly seduction.
The kings of the earth were immoral with her; earth-dwellers drunk with the wine of her immorality

Tyre "commits prostitution with all the kingdoms" by trade (Isaiah 23:17); Babylon made the nations drunk with her wine (Jeremiah 51:7). "Those who dwell on the earth" is a stock phrase in Revelation for unbelieving humanity (3:10; 6:10; 13:8).

Client kings and allied cities gained wealth and status by honouring Rome and the emperor, often through temples and festivals of the imperial cult; this was the "intoxicating" benefit of the Pax Romana.

Immorality here is mainly a metaphor for idolatrous and economic alliance with the city, though literal vice may be included. Many interpreters (Bauckham, Koester) stress the economic dimension that chapter 18 develops.
Some preterists read "kings of the earth" as "kings of the land": the Herodian rulers and Jerusalem's leaders who allied with Rome (Chilton).
World leaders who join the end-time religious and economic system.
Carried away in the Spirit into a wilderness

Ezekiel is repeatedly carried by the Spirit to see visions (Ezekiel 3:12-14; 8:3; 11:24; 43:5). Isaiah 21:1-10 is an oracle about "the wilderness of the sea", ending "Fallen, fallen is Babylon". The phrase "in the Spirit" marks major visions in Revelation (1:10; 4:2; 17:3; 21:10).

The wilderness setting draws on Isaiah 21 and contrasts with the "great, high mountain" from which John sees the New Jerusalem (21:10). It may also contrast with the woman of chapter 12, who is protected in the wilderness, whereas this woman will be left desolate (17:16).
A scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns
The beast is the sea beast of Revelation 13:1, which combines the four beasts of Daniel 7 and resembles the red dragon of 12:3. The ten horns come from Daniel's fourth beast (Daniel 7:7, 24).
Scarlet dye (from the kermes insect) was costly and associated with military commanders' cloaks and with royalty and wealth.

The woman rides the beast: she is carried and supported by the political-military power, but the arrangement is unstable, as 17:16 shows. Most interpreters see the beast as an imperial power (in John's day, Rome).

The beast is Rome (and Nero); the harlot riding it is Jerusalem, allied with and dependent on Rome against Christ and the church (Gentry). Preterists who identify Babylon with Rome instead see the city and its empire.
The Roman empire in its later, papal-supported form; the harlot (papal church) riding the secular powers of Europe (Barnes, Elliott).
The Antichrist and his revived Roman or world empire, supporting an apostate religious system (Walvoord).
Persecuting political power in every age, with seductive worldly culture riding on its back.
Covered with blasphemous names
The little horn speaks great things against the Most High (Daniel 7:8, 25; 11:36); the sea beast has blasphemous names on its heads (Revelation 13:1, 5-6).

Emperors bore divine titles on coins and inscriptions: divi filius (son of the deified one), Augustus (revered, sebastos), pontifex maximus, soter (saviour), kyrios (lord), and in some cities theos (god). Domitian reportedly encouraged "lord and god" (Suetonius, Domitian 13).
The beast claims for itself titles that belong to God alone. For first-century readers, imperial titles on coins in their purses were the obvious example.
Papal titles such as "Vicar of Christ", "Holy Father" and claims of universal headship were seen by historicists as blasphemous names.
The future Antichrist will claim divinity (2 Thessalonians 2:4).
Dressed in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold, precious stones and pearls

Purple, scarlet, gold and gems were materials of the tabernacle and the high priest's garments (Exodus 25:4; 28:5-8, 15-21). Jeremiah 4:30 pictures Jerusalem dressing in scarlet and gold to attract lovers who will kill her; Ezekiel 16:10-18 describes Jerusalem using God's gifts of fine clothing and jewels for her prostitution. The king of Tyre is covered with precious stones (Ezekiel 28:13).

Tyrian purple was the most expensive dye in the Roman world, reserved by law and custom for magistrates, senators and emperors; pearls were the supreme luxury (Pliny, Natural History 9.106-123). Courtesans displayed such finery.

Wealth, royalty and seductive luxury. The same list of colours and materials returns in the merchants' cargo (18:12) and their lament (18:16), and contrasts with the Bride, dressed in pure linen (19:8), and the New Jerusalem built of gold and jewels (21:18-21).
Gentry and Chilton read the colours as priestly and tabernacle colours (Exodus 28), pointing to Jerusalem and its priesthood corrupted into harlotry.
The scarlet and purple of cardinals and bishops and the wealth of the papal court were cited by Reformers and later historicists.
The wealth and splendour of the end-time religious and commercial system.
The alluring wealth and pomp of worldly power in every era.
A golden cup full of abominations and the impurities of her immorality

Babylon was "a golden cup in the LORD's hand, making all the earth drunk" (Jeremiah 51:7). "Abomination" (Hebrew to'evah, shiqquts) is the Old Testament term for idols and idolatrous practices (Deuteronomy 29:17; 1 Kings 11:5-7) and appears in Daniel's "abomination of desolation" (Daniel 9:27; 11:31; 12:11).
A golden drinking vessel spoke of extravagant banquets; libation bowls were used in pagan cult.
Outwardly splendid, inwardly corrupt: the cup offers luxury and belonging but contains idolatry and moral filth. Her cup is answered by the cup of God's wrath (16:19; 18:6).
Some preterists connect the cup with the temple vessels and the "abomination" language of Daniel and Matthew 24:15, applied to Jerusalem's corrupt worship.
Protestant interpreters connected the cup with the Mass chalice and the doctrines they regarded as corruptions.
On her forehead a name was written, a mystery

Jeremiah 3:3 speaks of Judah having "a prostitute's forehead" and refusing to blush. The high priest wore a golden plate on his forehead inscribed "Holy to the LORD" (Exodus 28:36-38). God's servants bear his name on their foreheads (Revelation 7:3; 14:1; 22:4), while the beast's followers bear its mark (13:16).

Some Roman writers mention prostitutes displaying their names publicly; Seneca refers to a name hanging over a prostitute's brow (Controversiae 1.2.7) and Juvenal describes Messalina using an assumed name in a brothel (Satires 6.122-123). How widely this applied is uncertain.
"Mystery" (Greek mysterion) may be part of the name or a note that the name is symbolic and must be interpreted (compare 17:7). The forehead name exposes her true identity.
A deliberate parody of the high priest's forehead plate: instead of "Holy to the LORD" the city bears "Babylon" (Chilton).
Some Protestant writers claimed that "Mysterium" had been inscribed on papal tiaras; this claim is disputed and poorly attested.

Historical Babylon was the empire that destroyed Jerusalem and the first temple (586 BC) and the archetype of proud, idolatrous world power (Genesis 11:1-9; Isaiah 13-14; 47; Jeremiah 50-51; Daniel 4:30, "Is this not great Babylon that I have built?"). After AD 70 Jewish apocalypses use "Babylon" as a code name for Rome, the second destroyer of the temple (4 Ezra 3:1-2, 28-31; 2 Baruch 11:1; 67:7; Sibylline Oracles 5.143, 159); 1 Peter 5:13 uses it for the city where Peter wrote. Jerusalem in turn is called "Sodom" and "Egypt" in Revelation 11:8 and treated as an apostate city in the prophets.

Rome was the dominant world city, centre of trade, empire and the imperial cult, built on seven hills; ancient Babylon was largely deserted by the first century (Strabo 16.1.5; Pliny, Natural History 6.122).

The identity of Babylon is disputed. Most critical and many evangelical scholars hold that in John's day Babylon was Rome, while noting that the image applies more broadly. Others hold it is Jerusalem, papal Rome, a future city, or the world system as such. Each reading appeals to different features of chapters 17-18.

Jerusalem (Gentry, Chilton, DeMar): "the great city" is where the Lord was crucified (11:8); the harlot image fits a covenant-breaking people; her priestly colours; she is drunk with the blood of prophets and saints, which Jesus laid at Jerusalem's door (Matthew 23:35-37; Luke 13:33); she rides (allies with) the beast Rome and is destroyed by it in AD 70; and she contrasts with the New Jerusalem. Other preterists identify Babylon with Rome and link its fall to the turmoil of AD 68-69 or to Rome's later judgment.

Papal Rome (the Reformers, Westminster-era Puritans, Newton, Elliott, Barnes): the city on seven hills that ruled the kings of Europe, whose church was seen as fallen into spiritual adultery and drunk with the blood of the martyrs of the Inquisition and the Reformation.

A future entity. Some read a literal rebuilt Babylon on the Euphrates in Iraq (Dyer, Woods, Thomas) on the ground that Isaiah 13 and Jeremiah 50-51 were never fully fulfilled; others (Walvoord) see an apostate world religion in chapter 17 and a commercial-political capital in chapter 18, possibly a revived Rome.

The world system of every age, human society organised in pride, luxury and idolatry against God; Rome was its form in John's day but Babylon reappears in every empire and culture (Hendriksen, Beale in part).

Rome in the first instance (the seven hills, the dominant world city, the code name in Jewish writings), and through Rome the recurring pattern of godless civilisation that will reach a final form before Christ returns (Beale, Osborne, Bauckham, Koester).
The mother of prostitutes and of the abominations of the earth
"Like mother, like daughter" is said of Jerusalem in Ezekiel 16:44-45. Babylon at Babel is the origin of human pride against God (Genesis 11).
Rome was hailed as mother of cities and of nations (Roma as mater); colonies were her "daughters".
She is the source and prototype of idolatry and corruption, spreading them to others. The title parodies honorific civic titles.
The Church of Rome as "mother church" whose daughters share her errors; some later historicists extended "daughters" to state churches that retained Roman practices.
Jerusalem as the mother city of Judaism, whose apostasy was the root of persecution of the church (Chilton).
Drunk with the blood of the saints and witnesses of Jesus

Jesus said that all the righteous blood shed on earth would come on Jerusalem and on "this generation" (Matthew 23:35-37) and that a prophet could not perish outside Jerusalem (Luke 13:33). Isaiah 34:5-7 speaks of a sword drunk with blood; oppressors drunk on their own blood (Isaiah 49:26). Revelation 18:24 echoes the charge.

Nero's persecution in Rome after the fire of AD 64 killed a great multitude of Christians (Tacitus, Annals 15.44; 1 Clement 5-6), including, by tradition, Peter and Paul. Local persecutions in Asia (Antipas at Pergamum, Revelation 2:13) also form the background.
The city delights in the deaths of the faithful as a drunkard delights in wine. John's "great amazement" (17:6) is perhaps because she appears so attractive.

Jerusalem: from Stephen (Acts 7) to James (Acts 12; Josephus, Antiquities 20.200), Jerusalem's leaders persecuted the church, and Jesus explicitly laid the blood of the prophets at Jerusalem's door (Gentry).
Papal Rome, held responsible for the deaths of Waldensians, Albigensians, Lollards, Hussites and Protestants.
The end-time religious system that persecutes tribulation believers.
Rome under Nero and later emperors, and every power that persecutes Christians.
The beast that was, and is not, and is about to come up out of the Abyss

It is a parody of God's name, "who is and who was and who is to come" (Revelation 1:4, 8; 4:8), and of the Lamb who was dead and lives (1:18; 2:8). The beast's "fatal wound that was healed" (13:3, 12, 14) is the same idea. The abyss is the prison of demonic powers (9:1-11; 11:7; 20:1-3; compare 1 Enoch 10:4-6; 18:11-16).

After Nero's suicide in AD 68 many believed he was alive or would return; several pretenders appeared in the east (Tacitus, Histories 2.8-9; Suetonius, Nero 57; Dio Cassius 64.9; 66.19). Jewish and Christian Sibylline Oracles turned him into a returning eschatological enemy (Sibylline Oracles 4.119-139; 5.137-154, 361-385; later Ascension of Isaiah 4:2-4).

The beast imitates resurrection: it appears to die and returns from the abyss, but its destiny is destruction (Greek apoleia, 17:8, 11). Many scholars think John uses the Nero legend; others think the "death and return" refers to the empire rather than a person.
The Roman empire "died" in the chaos of AD 68-69 after Nero's death and "revived" under Vespasian (Gentry); the beast was Nero as head of Rome.
Pagan imperial Rome that fell (AD 476) and revived as the papal and Holy Roman power.
The future Antichrist, who may suffer an apparent death and revival, or the Roman empire that ceased and will be revived in the last days (Walvoord).
Persecuting power in every age seems to be defeated and then reappears in new forms, until its final destruction.
John uses the Nero redivivus legend as a symbol: the persecuting emperor returns in Domitian or in a future Nero-like figure (Bauckham, Aune, Koester).
Whose names were not written in the Book of Life from the foundation of the world

God keeps a book of the living (Exodus 32:32-33; Psalm 69:28; Isaiah 4:3; Daniel 12:1; Malachi 3:16). Jewish texts speak of heavenly books recording the righteous and the deeds of all (1 Enoch 47:3; 108:3; Jubilees 30:20-22). Revelation 13:8 calls it "the book of life of the Lamb who was slain".
Greek cities kept citizen registers, and a condemned citizen's name could be erased.

The faithful are secure because God enrolled them from the beginning; the world "marvels" at the beast because it has no anchor in God. The phrase raises questions of predestination that interpreters answer differently.
This calls for a mind with wisdom

The same call to wisdom introduces the number of the beast (Revelation 13:18). Daniel says the wise will understand (Daniel 12:10); the maskilim (wise teachers) of Daniel 11:33-35 instruct the people under persecution.
The reader is invited to decode the symbol. The decoding is itself symbolic and layered: the heads are both mountains and kings. Interpreters agree that John signals a puzzle, not on how to solve it.
The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits

In the prophets mountains can symbolise kingdoms: the stone becomes a mountain filling the earth (Daniel 2:35, 44-45); Babylon is a "destroying mountain" (Jeremiah 51:25); the mountain of the LORD's house (Isaiah 2:2). Jerusalem was built on hills (Psalm 125:2), and some later Jewish texts count seven, though this is late and uncertain.

Rome was proverbially "the city of seven hills" (Palatine, Capitoline, Quirinal, Viminal, Esquiline, Caelian, Aventine), a commonplace in Latin poets (Virgil, Georgics 2.535; Horace, Carmen Saeculare 7; Propertius 3.11.57; Martial 4.64) and celebrated in the Septimontium. A sestertius of Vespasian (AD 71) shows Roma seated on seven hills.
For most interpreters this is the clearest pointer to Rome in the chapter. The "mountains" are immediately explained also as kings, so the image may be political rather than topographical.
Gentry agrees the seven mountains are Rome, but notes they belong to the beast, not the woman: the harlot (Jerusalem) "sits" on Rome in the sense of being allied with and supported by it.
Rome, seat of the papacy, confirming the identification of Babylon with papal Rome (Barnes, Elliott).
Many futurists read mountains as kingdoms (Daniel 2): seven world empires through history (Walvoord); others accept a reference to Rome and expect a revived Rome.
The completeness of worldly power on which the seductive world culture rests.
A deliberate reference to Rome that also symbolises the fullness of political power (Beale, Bauckham).
Seven kings: five have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come
Daniel 7:17 explains beasts as kings, and Daniel 8 and 11 list successive rulers. The number seven may be literal or symbolic of completeness.

Lists of Roman emperors differ on where to start (Julius Caesar or Augustus) and whether to count the brief rulers of AD 68-69 (Galba, Otho, Vitellius). Ancient writers such as Suetonius (The Twelve Caesars) and the Sibylline Oracles (5.12-51) began with Julius; Tacitus (Annals 1.1) begins the principate with Augustus.

The verse is a key text for dating Revelation, and it is disputed. If "one is" can be identified, it dates the book. But many scholars think the seven are symbolic, meaning the series of rulers is nearly complete and the end is near.

Counting from Julius Caesar: Julius, Augustus, Tiberius, Gaius (Caligula) and Claudius have fallen; Nero "is"; Galba, who reigned only seven months, is the one who "remains a little while". This supports a date before AD 68 (Gentry, Before Jerusalem Fell).

Late-date scholars either count from Augustus and skip the three brief rulers, making Vespasian the one who "is" and Titus the short-lived seventh, with Domitian as the eighth (Nero returned in spirit); or regard the seven as symbolic of the whole series of emperors (Bauckham, Aune, Beale, Koester).

Seven forms of Roman government listed by Livy and Tacitus (kings, consuls, decemvirs, dictators, military tribunes, emperors, and a seventh short-lived form), with the papacy as the eighth (Barnes, Elliott).
Seven successive world empires: Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Persia, Greece (fallen), Rome (is), and a future kingdom, with the Antichrist's empire as the eighth (Walvoord and others).
Seven is the number of completeness; the kings stand for the whole sequence of world powers that oppose God, and the end is always near (Hendriksen).
The beast is an eighth king, who belongs to the seven and goes to destruction

Daniel's little horn arises after the ten and is different from them (Daniel 7:8, 24). Early Christian numerology saw eight as the number of resurrection (the eighth day, Sunday), and the beast parodies Christ's resurrection.

The Nero redivivus legend pictured Nero returning as a new ruler after the others. Bauckham notes that Neron Kaisar in Hebrew letters sums to 666 and that 888 was used by some early Christians for the name of Jesus in Greek, so "eighth" may be part of a parody.
The beast is one of the seven returning as an eighth: an evil ruler revived. Its destiny is destruction.
Either Vespasian as the revival of the empire after Nero, or Rome itself as the beast that sums up the seven heads (Gentry).
The papacy, which inherited the power of imperial Rome while being a new form.
The future Antichrist, either a revived ruler from history or one who rules after a seventh world empire (Walvoord).
A Nero-like emperor (Domitian for many late-date scholars) or a final Antichrist figure modelled on Nero (Bauckham, Aune).
The persistent spirit of antichristian power, which always "belongs to" the earlier powers and always heads for ruin.
The ten horns are ten kings who have not yet received a kingdom
Daniel 7:7-8, 20, 24: the fourth beast has ten horns, ten kings who arise from that kingdom. "Horn" symbolises power (Psalm 75:10; Zechariah 1:18-21).
Rome ruled through provincial governors and client kings. The Nero legend in the Sibylline Oracles pictured him returning with eastern (Parthian) kings to destroy Rome.

Subordinate rulers who give their power to the beast for a short time and join it in opposing the Lamb. Ten probably signals completeness of earthly powers rather than an exact count, though futurists often take it literally.
Rulers of the Roman provinces or client kings who joined Rome against Jerusalem in AD 66-70 (Chilton, Gentry).
The ten Germanic kingdoms that arose from the break-up of the western Roman empire (Vandals, Ostrogoths, Franks, and others), which supported the papacy (Elliott, Barnes, Newton).
A future ten-nation confederacy, often a revived Roman empire in Europe or the Mediterranean, that hands power to the Antichrist (Walvoord).
All the powers of the earth that ally with antichristian authority in every age.
Allies of a returning Nero-like emperor (eastern kings), used symbolically for all rulers who support the beast (Bauckham, Aune).
One hour of authority as kings, along with the beast
Daniel 4:19 (Greek text) uses "one hour" for a short time; the prophets use "hour" for the appointed time of judgment. "One hour" recurs for Babylon's sudden fall (18:10, 17, 19).
A very short period of power: the alliance against the Lamb is brief and doomed.
The Lamb will triumph, because He is Lord of lords and King of kings

Deuteronomy 10:17 ("God of gods and Lord of lords"); Psalm 136:2-3; the Greek of Daniel 4:37 calls God "God of gods, Lord of lords and King of kings". 1 Enoch 9:4 and 2 Maccabees 13:4 use similar titles. "King of kings" was the title of Babylonian and Persian monarchs (Ezekiel 26:7; Ezra 7:12; Daniel 2:37).
Parthian rulers used "king of kings" on their coins; Roman emperors were acclaimed lords. The Lamb outranks them all.
Divine titles given to the Lamb. The title is reversed in 19:16 (King of kings and Lord of lords). The war is won by the Lamb, whose weapon is his sacrificial death and his word (19:15).
Those with Him are called and chosen and faithful

"Many are called but few are chosen" (Matthew 22:14). Israel was God's chosen people (Deuteronomy 7:6); the War Scroll at Qumran describes the "chosen ones" fighting in the final war of the sons of light (1QM 12:1-5).
The Lamb's companions share his victory. Unlike the War Scroll, Revelation's saints conquer by faithfulness and witness, not by arms (12:11).
The armies of heaven, including the glorified church, returning with Christ (19:14).
All faithful believers who share Christ's victory throughout history.
The ten horns and the beast will hate the prostitute, make her desolate and naked, eat her flesh and burn her with fire

Ezekiel 16:37-41 and 23:25-29 describe Jerusalem's lovers turning on her, stripping her naked and burning her houses; Jeremiah 4:30 says her lovers will seek her life. Eating flesh recalls Jezebel devoured by dogs (2 Kings 9:36) and Micah 3:3. Leviticus 21:9 decrees that a priest's daughter who prostitutes herself must be burned with fire.
Rome was burned in the great fire of AD 64; the Capitol was burned during the civil war in December 69. The Nero legend in the Sibylline Oracles imagined Nero returning to burn Rome.

Evil is self-destructive: the political power that carried the seductive city turns against her. This is one of the most important verses for the identity debate, because the city is destroyed by the beast itself.

Rome (the beast) and its allies destroyed Jerusalem (the harlot) in AD 70, burning the city and temple; the Ezekiel 16 and 23 background and the priestly burning law (Leviticus 21:9) fit Jerusalem precisely (Gentry, Chilton).
The nations of Europe turning on the papacy: the Reformation, the French Revolution's confiscation of church property, and the loss of the Papal States (1870).
The Antichrist and his ten kings will destroy the apostate world church (ecclesiastical Babylon) at mid-tribulation to demand worship for himself (Walvoord).
The world's political powers ultimately destroy the very culture of luxury and idolatry they supported; evil devours itself.
For those who identify Babylon with Rome, it pictures a returning Nero with eastern allies destroying Rome, a symbol of the self-destruction of empire (Bauckham, Aune).
God has put it into their hearts to carry out His purpose

God uses pagan powers as instruments of judgment: Assyria the rod of his anger (Isaiah 10:5-7), Nebuchadnezzar "my servant" (Jeremiah 25:9), Cyrus his anointed (Isaiah 45:1). He hardened Pharaoh's heart (Exodus 9:12) and moves the hearts of kings (Proverbs 21:1).
God's sovereignty extends even over the alliance of evil: its unity and its self-destruction both serve his purpose until his words are fulfilled.
The woman is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth

"The great city" is Jerusalem in Revelation 11:8 ("where their Lord was crucified") and Babylon in 14:8; 16:19; 18:10, 16, 18, 19, 21. Jeremiah 22:8 calls Jerusalem "this great city"; Jonah calls Nineveh "that great city" (Jonah 1:2). Lamentations 1:1 calls Jerusalem "great among the nations" and "princess among the provinces".
In John's time only Rome ruled over the kings of the earth in an obvious sense; client kings like Herod Agrippa held their thrones at Rome's pleasure.

The final explanation identifies the woman as a city with dominion over the world's rulers. For most interpreters it settles the matter in favour of Rome (or a future world capital); preterists who favour Jerusalem read the rule as covenantal or religious.

Gentry argues that Jerusalem held a covenantal kingship over the nations as the city of the great King (Psalm 48:2) and was the centre of the Jewish world; Chilton translates "kings of the land". Critics answer that the plain sense of rule over the kings of the earth fits Rome far better; preterists reply that 11:8 already defines "the great city" as Jerusalem.
Papal Rome, which in the Middle Ages claimed authority over the kings of Christendom, crowning and deposing them.
A future world capital, either a rebuilt Babylon or a revived Rome, ruling the nations in the last days.
The world city of every age, whose cultural and economic power holds sway over the rulers of the earth.
Rome, the ruling city of John's world, and its successors (Bauckham, Koester, Beale).

Gentry, Chilton, DeMar and others hold that the harlot is first-century Jerusalem and the beast is Rome. The harlot's priestly colours, her guilt for the blood of the prophets, her alliance with Rome (sitting on the beast) and her destruction by Rome in AD 70 all fit Jerusalem, and she is set against the New Jerusalem, the Bride. The seven kings are the Julio-Claudian emperors with Nero as the sixth, which supports a pre-70 date. Some other preterists and many early-date scholars instead identify Babylon with Rome and read the chapter as predicting Rome's judgment.

Shares the Jerusalem identification and sees the fall of the harlot in AD 70 as the end of the old covenant age and the marriage of the Lamb to the new covenant bride (Preston, King). Critics note this view collapses the future consummation into AD 70, against the historic creeds; proponents say the imminence language of Revelation requires it.

Babylon is papal Rome, the apostate church of the city on seven hills that ruled the kings of Europe and shed the blood of the martyrs. The beast is the Roman power in its papal phase, the ten horns are the barbarian kingdoms that succeeded Rome, and the beast's turning on the harlot is the gradual stripping of papal power by the nations (Luther, the Reformers, Newton, Elliott, Barnes).

The chapter describes the end time. Walvoord identifies the harlot with a future apostate world religion that supports and then is destroyed by the Antichrist and his ten-nation confederation; others (Dyer, Woods, Thomas) see a literal rebuilt Babylon in Iraq. The seven heads are successive world empires and the eighth the Antichrist's kingdom. Historic premillennialists (Ladd) see an end-time manifestation of the Rome-like world power.

Babylon is the world as seductress in every age, the culture of luxury, power and false religion that draws people from God, while the beast is persecuting political power. Rome was the form both took in John's day. Their mutual destruction shows that evil is self-defeating (Hendriksen, Milligan).

Most modern commentators (Bauckham, Aune, Koester, Beale, Osborne) see Rome as the first referent: the city on seven hills, the world ruler and the city Jewish writers called Babylon. The chapter also exposes a recurring pattern that will reach a final form at the end; the Nero redivivus legend shapes the riddle of the beast.
List the clues in chapter 17 that point to Rome and those that point to Jerusalem. Which do you find strongest, and why?
Why does John portray Babylon as a prostitute and the New Jerusalem as a bride? What does the contrast teach about the church's relation to its culture?
How does the riddle of the seven kings (17:10) bear on the date of Revelation? Is it possible to count the kings with confidence?
What does it mean that the beast and the ten kings turn on the prostitute (17:16), and that God put it in their hearts (17:17)?
In what ways might "Babylon" be present in the economic and political life of today's world, whichever historical identification is correct?
The Fall of Babylon: Laments of Kings, Merchants and Sailors

A glorious angel announces that Babylon the great has fallen and become a haunt of demons and unclean creatures, because the nations, kings and merchants were intoxicated and enriched by her. Another voice calls God's people to come out of her, and calls for her to be repaid double for her pride and luxury, since she boasted she sat as a queen and would never mourn. Three groups who profited from her stand at a distance and lament: the kings of the earth, the merchants, whose long cargo list catalogues the luxuries of the world ending with human beings, and the shipmasters and sailors. Heaven, the saints, apostles and prophets are told to rejoice, and a mighty angel hurls a millstone into the sea as a sign that the city will be thrown down and silenced: no music, craft, mill, lamp or wedding. Her guilt is her sorcery and the blood of prophets, saints and all the slain.
